topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The federal Fair Housing Act is Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 and is codified in the U.S. Code beginning at which section?
explanation: The Fair Housing Act (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968) is codified at 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq. (42 U.S.C. § 1981/1982 is the separate Civil Rights Act of 1866; 15 U.S.C. § 1 is the Sherman Antitrust Act; 42 U.S.C. § 12101 is the ADA.)
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Chapter 45 (uscode.house.gov); DOJ Civil Rights Division, 'The Fair Housing Act.'

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: As originally enacted in 1968, the Fair Housing Act prohibited housing discrimination based on which set of classes?
choice_a: Race, color, religion, and national origin only
choice_b: Race, color, religion, national origin, and sex
choice_c: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, and handicap
choice_d: Race and national origin only
explanation: The original 1968 Act protected race, color, religion, and national origin; sex was added in 1974. Familial status and handicap (disability) were not added until the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, bringing the total to seven protected classes.
source_note: DOJ Civil Rights Division, 'The Fair Housing Act'; 42 U.S.C. § 3604 legislative history.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 expanded the federal Fair Housing Act's protected classes to seven by adding which two categories?
choice_a: Sexual orientation and gender identity
choice_b: Marital status and source of income
choice_c: Familial status and handicap (disability)
choice_d: Age and veteran status
explanation: The 1988 Amendments added familial status (protecting families with children) and handicap/disability, bringing federal protected classes to seven: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and handicap.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, Pub. L. 100-430.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, which of the following is NOT a protected class?
choice_a: Familial status
choice_b: National origin
choice_c: Handicap
choice_d: Marital status
explanation: Marital status is not one of the seven federal protected classes (race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, handicap). Some states and localities add marital status by their own statutes, but it is not federally protected under 42 U.S.C. § 3604.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity overview of protected classes.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A tenant is denied a rental unit solely because her only income is a Section 8 housing choice voucher. Under the federal Fair Housing Act alone, has an actionable violation occurred?
choice_a: No, because source of income is not among the seven federal protected classes (though some states/localities separately protect it)
choice_b: Yes, because source of income is a federal protected class
choice_c: Yes, because vouchers are treated as a form of familial status
choice_d: No, because federal law never restricts a landlord's tenant selection
explanation: Source of income is not a federally protected class under the Fair Housing Act. A number of states and cities have enacted their own laws barring source-of-income discrimination, but no federal Fair Housing Act claim exists based on source of income alone.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604 (seven federal classes only); HUD guidance distinguishing federal vs. state/local protected classes.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bostock v. Clayton County (2020), how has HUD approached claims of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity under the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: HUD has stated the Fair Housing Act can never apply to sexual orientation or gender identity under any circumstance
choice_b: HUD takes the position that discrimination because of sexual orientation or gender identity can constitute discrimination 'because of sex' and investigates such complaints, even though those terms do not appear explicitly in the statutory text
choice_c: Congress amended 42 U.S.C. § 3604 in 2020 to add sexual orientation and gender identity as freestanding protected classes
choice_d: The issue is governed exclusively by the ADA, not the Fair Housing Act
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's text does not list sexual orientation or gender identity as separate protected classes. However, after Bostock v. Clayton County held that Title VII's 'because of sex' language covers sexual orientation and gender identity, HUD issued guidance applying that reasoning to the Fair Housing Act's sex discrimination provisions and accepts/investigates such complaints under the 'sex' category.
source_note: Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644 (2020); HUD memorandum applying Bostock to Fair Housing Act enforcement (2021).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Section 3604(a) of the Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to do which of the following based on a protected class?
choice_a: Charge different security deposits for the same unit
choice_b: Print a discriminatory statement in a newspaper advertisement
choice_c: Refuse to sell or rent, or otherwise make a dwelling unavailable, after a bona fide offer
choice_d: Refuse to lend money for the purchase of a home
explanation: Section 3604(a) prohibits refusing to sell or rent, or otherwise making a dwelling unavailable, to any person because of a protected class. Discriminatory terms/conditions fall under 3604(b), discriminatory advertising under 3604(c), and lending discrimination under the separate Section 3605.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A landlord rents identical units to all applicants but requires a double security deposit and an extra $50/month rent only from families with children. This practice most directly violates which provision of the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: Section 3604(a) - refusal to rent
choice_b: Section 3605 - residential real estate-related transactions
choice_c: Section 3607 - religious exemption
choice_d: Section 3604(b) - discriminatory terms, conditions, or privileges
explanation: Section 3604(b) prohibits discriminating in the terms, conditions, or privileges of a rental (or the provision of services/facilities) because of a protected class, including familial status. Charging different deposits or rent to families with children based solely on that status is a classic 3604(b) violation.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: It is unlawful under Section 3604(c) of the Fair Housing Act to publish or cause to be published which type of statement?
choice_a: Any notice, statement, or advertisement indicating a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class
choice_b: Any statement of the seller's asking price
choice_c: Any statement disclosing square footage
choice_d: Any statement identifying the listing broker
explanation: Section 3604(c) prohibits making, printing, or publishing (or causing to be made, printed, or published) any notice, statement, or advertisement indicating a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin. It applies regardless of the advertiser's intent.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A listing agent truthfully tells a prospective Hispanic buyer that a home 'just sold' when it is, in fact, still available, in order to discourage the buyer from pursuing it. This is an example of a violation of which section of the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: Section 3606 - discrimination in brokerage services
choice_b: Section 3604(d) - false representation that a dwelling is unavailable for inspection, sale, or rental
choice_c: Section 3607 - exemptions
choice_d: Section 3603 - effective dates
explanation: Section 3604(d) makes it unlawful to represent to any person, because of a protected class, that a dwelling is not available for inspection, sale, or rental when in fact it is available.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: An agent visits homeowners in a changing neighborhood and warns them that property values will soon plummet because families of a particular race are moving in, urging them to sell quickly. This practice is known as:
choice_a: Steering
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Blockbusting
choice_d: Tie-in selling
explanation: Blockbusting (also called panic peddling) is prohibited by Section 3604(e), which bars inducing or attempting to induce a person to sell or rent by representations regarding the entry (or prospective entry) of persons of a particular protected class into the neighborhood.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A real estate agent, without being asked, consistently shows Asian-American buyers only listings in neighborhoods with large Asian-American populations and avoids showing them listings elsewhere. This practice is called:
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: Group boycott
choice_d: Steering
explanation: Steering is the practice of directing homebuyers or renters toward or away from particular neighborhoods based on a protected class. Courts have held that steering violates Section 3604(a) because it effectively makes housing in other areas unavailable to the steered buyer.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a); federal case law interpreting steering as unlawful 'making unavailable.'

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A mortgage lender refuses to make any loans on properties located within a certain zip code because the area's population is predominantly minority, regardless of individual applicants' creditworthiness. This practice is called:
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: Puffing
explanation: Redlining is denying or limiting financial services (loans, insurance, etc.) for properties in specific geographic areas based on the racial or ethnic composition of that area, rather than the qualifications of individual applicants. It is prohibited under Section 3605's ban on discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Section 3605 of the Fair Housing Act specifically prohibits discrimination based on a protected class in which category of activity?
choice_a: Zoning and land use decisions by local governments
choice_b: Residential real estate-related transactions, including the making or purchasing of loans and the provision of appraisals
choice_c: Employment decisions within a real estate brokerage
choice_d: Advertising placed in newspapers only
explanation: Section 3605 prohibits discrimination by any person or entity whose business includes engaging in residential real estate-related transactions, which includes making or purchasing loans, selling/brokering loans, and appraising residential real property.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Section 3606 of the Fair Housing Act addresses discrimination in which activity?
choice_a: The financing of home purchases
choice_b: Zoning variances
choice_c: Access to or membership in multiple listing services and other real-estate-related brokerage organizations
choice_d: Design and construction of new multifamily housing
explanation: Section 3606 prohibits denying any person access to, or membership or participation in, a multiple listing service, real estate brokers' organization, or other real-estate-related service, organization, or facility, on the basis of a protected class.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following is a hallmark of the 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption found in Section 3603(b)(2) of the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: It exempts any landlord who owns fewer than 25 rental units nationwide
choice_b: It exempts all religious organizations from every provision of the Act
choice_c: It exempts any transaction handled without a written lease
choice_d: It exempts rooms or units in a dwelling of four or fewer units if the owner actually occupies one of the units as their residence
explanation: The so-called 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption applies to owner-occupied buildings with no more than four units, where the owner lives in one of the units. It does not exempt discriminatory advertising under 3604(c), and it never exempts race or color discrimination (which remains barred by the separate Civil Rights Act of 1866).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Fair Housing Act's exemption for the private sale of a single-family home by its owner (Section 3603(b)(1)) requires all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: The buyer must be a first-time homebuyer
choice_b: The owner does not own more than three such single-family houses at one time
choice_c: The sale is made without the use of a real estate broker, agent, or salesperson
choice_d: No discriminatory advertising is used in connection with the sale
explanation: The private-sale exemption requires the owner not own more than three such houses at a time, forgo the services of a licensee, and avoid discriminatory advertising. There is no requirement about the buyer's status as a first-time buyer.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under Section 3607, a religious organization that owns and operates non-commercial housing may restrict occupancy to members of its own religion UNLESS:
choice_a: The building has more than four units
choice_b: Membership in the religion is itself restricted on account of race, color, or national origin
choice_c: The organization is tax-exempt
choice_d: The building was constructed before 1968
explanation: Section 3607 permits religious organizations to give a preference to members of their own religion for non-commercial housing they own or operate, but this exemption is unavailable if the religion itself restricts membership based on race, color, or national origin.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A bona fide private club that is not open to the public may, under Section 3607, limit the rental or occupancy of lodgings it owns for other than a commercial purpose to:
choice_a: Persons of a single race only, regardless of membership rules
choice_b: Any person, since private clubs are entirely outside the Act
choice_c: Its own members
choice_d: Only families without children
explanation: The private club exemption in Section 3607 allows a bona fide private club to limit non-commercial lodging it owns to its own members. It does not create a blanket exemption for race discrimination, which is never permitted under the Act or the Civil Rights Act of 1866.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: No exemption under the Fair Housing Act - including the Mrs. Murphy exemption or the private-sale-by-owner exemption - can ever excuse discrimination based on which protected class?
choice_a: Familial status
choice_b: Handicap
choice_c: Sex
choice_d: Race or color
explanation: The separate Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. § 1982), as interpreted in Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968), bars all racial discrimination in property transactions with no exemptions whatsoever. So even where a Fair Housing Act exemption applies, discrimination based on race or color remains illegal under the 1866 Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 1982; Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A retirement community wants to qualify for the 'housing for older persons' exemption from familial status discrimination by having at least 80% of its occupied units house at least one person 55 or older. What is this exemption commonly called?
choice_a: The Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) '55 or older' exemption
choice_b: The Mrs. Murphy exemption
choice_c: The private club exemption
choice_d: The reasonable accommodation exemption
explanation: The Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995 (HOPA) allows a '55 or older' community to be exempt from familial status discrimination claims if at least 80% of occupied units have at least one occupant age 55 or older, and the community publishes and adheres to policies demonstrating an intent to house persons 55 and older, among other requirements.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A community that requires 100% of its occupied units to be occupied by at least one person age 62 or older can qualify for the 'housing for older persons' exemption without needing to meet the 80% occupancy test that applies to 55-or-older communities. This exemption applies to which type of discrimination claim?
choice_a: It exempts the community from all seven protected classes
choice_b: It exempts the community from familial status discrimination claims only
choice_c: It exempts the community from race discrimination claims
choice_d: It exempts the community from handicap discrimination claims only
explanation: The '62 or older' housing exemption (requiring 100% of units occupied by at least one person 62+) - like the '55 or older' exemption - exempts a qualifying community only from familial status discrimination. It provides no exemption from race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or handicap discrimination.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, 'familial status' protects which of the following groups from discrimination?
choice_a: Only married couples with biological children
choice_b: Only single parents
choice_c: One or more individuals under 18 living with a parent or legal custodian, pregnant women, and any person in the process of securing legal custody of a minor
choice_d: Any household with more than two occupants
explanation: 'Familial status' is defined broadly to include one or more children under 18 living with a parent or person with legal custody, a pregnant woman, and any person in the process of securing legal custody (e.g., through adoption) of a child under 18.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, a person has a 'handicap' (disability) if they have a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, have a record of such an impairment, or are regarded as having such an impairment. Which of the following is specifically EXCLUDED from this definition?
choice_a: A person recovering from alcoholism
choice_b: A person with a mobility impairment
choice_c: A person with a mental illness
choice_d: Current, illegal use of a controlled substance
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's definition of 'handicap' explicitly excludes current, illegal use of or addiction to a controlled substance. Recovering alcoholics, and persons with physical or mental impairments generally, are covered.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What is the key legal distinction between a 'reasonable accommodation' and a 'reasonable modification' under the Fair Housing Act's handicap provisions?
choice_a: A reasonable accommodation is a change to a rule, policy, practice, or service; a reasonable modification is a structural or physical change to the premises
choice_b: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable under the Act
choice_c: A reasonable accommodation only applies to buyers, while a reasonable modification only applies to renters
choice_d: A reasonable accommodation requires a doctor's note, but a reasonable modification never does
explanation: A 'reasonable accommodation' is a change to a rule, policy, practice, or service (e.g., allowing an assistance animal despite a no-pets policy). A 'reasonable modification' is a structural change to the dwelling or common areas (e.g., installing a wheelchair ramp) to afford a person with a disability full use of the premises.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A)-(B); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004) and Reasonable Modifications (2008).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, who is generally responsible for the cost of a reasonable modification (e.g., widening a doorway) requested by a tenant with a disability in privately-owned, non-federally-assisted housing?
choice_a: The landlord must always pay for reasonable modifications
choice_b: The tenant is generally responsible for the cost of the modification, though the landlord must permit it
choice_c: HUD reimburses the landlord automatically
choice_d: The cost must be split 50/50 between landlord and tenant
explanation: In privately owned, non-federally-funded housing, the landlord must permit a reasonable modification at the tenant's own expense. By contrast, reasonable accommodations (policy changes) are generally made at the landlord's expense. In federally-assisted housing, the landlord may bear modification costs.
source_note: HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Modifications (2008); 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A rental community has a strict 'no pets' policy. A prospective tenant with a documented anxiety disorder requests to keep an assistance animal that helps manage her condition. Under fair housing law, the landlord should treat this request as:
choice_a: A pet request that can be denied under the no-pets policy
choice_b: Grounds for automatic denial because emotional support animals are never covered by federal law
choice_c: A request for a reasonable accommodation, which generally must be granted, and the animal is not treated as a 'pet' for policy or fee purposes
choice_d: A request that requires ADA-mandated public access rights
explanation: Assistance animals (including emotional support animals) that provide disability-related assistance are treated as a reasonable accommodation request under the Fair Housing Act, not as 'pets' - a no-pets policy cannot be used to deny them, and pet fees/deposits generally may not be charged.
source_note: HUD Notice FHEO-2020-01, Assessing a Person's Request to Have an Animal as a Reasonable Accommodation; 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: When a tenant's disability and disability-related need for an assistance animal are not obvious, what may a housing provider ask for when evaluating a reasonable accommodation request?
choice_a: The tenant's complete medical records and specific diagnosis
choice_b: Nothing at all; the provider must accept every request without question
choice_c: Proof that the animal has completed a certified training and registration program
choice_d: Reliable documentation confirming the disability-related need for the animal, without demanding the specific diagnosis or detailed medical history
explanation: Where the disability or disability-related need is not obvious, a housing provider may request reliable documentation supporting the need for the accommodation, but may not demand detailed medical records, a specific diagnosis, or animal certification/registration, which are not required under federal guidance.
source_note: HUD Notice FHEO-2020-01, Assessing a Person's Request to Have an Animal as a Reasonable Accommodation.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements for accessibility apply to covered multifamily dwellings of four or more units for which first occupied after a specific date?
choice_a: March 13, 1991
choice_b: January 1, 1968
choice_d: January 1, 2000
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's accessible design and construction requirements apply to covered multifamily dwellings of four or more units designed and constructed for first occupancy after March 13, 1991.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following is NOT one of the Fair Housing Act's seven basic design and construction accessibility requirements for covered new multifamily housing?
choice_a: An accessible building entrance on an accessible route
choice_b: A minimum of one designated accessible parking space per every unit in the building
choice_c: Reinforced bathroom walls to allow later installation of grab bars
choice_d: Light switches, outlets, and thermostats in accessible locations
explanation: The seven requirements cover an accessible entrance, accessible common/public use areas, usable doors, an accessible route into and through the unit, accessible environmental controls, reinforced bathroom walls for grab bars, and usable kitchens and bathrooms. A specific per-unit accessible parking ratio is not one of the seven statutory requirements.
source_note: HUD/DOJ, Fair Housing Act Design Manual; 24 C.F.R. § 100.205.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: For a covered multifamily building with an elevator, how many units must meet the Fair Housing Act's accessibility design requirements?
choice_a: Only the ground-floor units
choice_b: None, since elevator buildings are exempt
choice_c: All units in the building
choice_d: Only 10% of the units
explanation: In a covered multifamily building served by an elevator, all units must meet the Fair Housing Act's accessibility requirements. In buildings without an elevator, only the ground-floor units (including ground-floor units at different levels) must be accessible.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What is the deadline for filing an administrative housing discrimination complaint with HUD under the Fair Housing Act, measured from the date of the alleged discriminatory act?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 2 years
choice_c: 5 years
choice_d: 1 year
explanation: A person alleging a discriminatory housing practice generally has one year from the occurrence or termination of the alleged discriminatory act to file an administrative complaint with HUD.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Separate from filing an administrative complaint with HUD, an aggrieved person may bring a private civil action in federal or state court under the Fair Housing Act within how long after the alleged discriminatory act?
choice_a: 2 years
choice_b: 90 days
choice_c: 6 months
choice_d: 10 years
explanation: An aggrieved person may commence a civil action in an appropriate federal or state court within two years after the occurrence or termination of the alleged discriminatory housing practice, regardless of whether an administrative complaint was also filed with HUD.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: After a Fair Housing Act complaint is filed with HUD, HUD is generally required to complete its investigation within approximately how many days, absent good cause for extension?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 100 days
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: One year
explanation: The Fair Housing Act directs HUD to complete the investigation of a complaint within 100 days after it is filed, unless it is impracticable to do so, and to attempt conciliation throughout the process.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: In a private civil lawsuit under the Fair Housing Act (as opposed to a HUD administrative proceeding), a prevailing plaintiff may potentially recover which of the following?
choice_a: Only injunctive relief, with no monetary damages ever available
choice_b: Only the return of a security deposit
choice_c: Actual damages, injunctive or other equitable relief, and, in appropriate cases, punitive damages
choice_d: Criminal fines paid directly to the plaintiff
explanation: In a civil action under the Fair Housing Act, courts may award actual and punitive damages, as well as permanent or temporary injunctive relief. Punitive damages are generally not available against the government in HUD administrative proceedings but can be awarded in private civil suits.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under fair housing law, a 'tester' is best described as:
choice_a: A government auditor who inspects properties for building code violations
choice_b: A licensed appraiser who verifies property condition
choice_c: A HUD employee who administers licensing exams
choice_d: A person who, without a genuine intent to rent or buy, poses as a prospective tenant or buyer to gather evidence of discriminatory practices
explanation: Fair housing 'testers' pose as renters or buyers - without any genuine intent to rent or purchase - specifically to detect and document unlawful discriminatory conduct. Courts have recognized that testers have standing to bring Fair Housing Act claims even absent a real intent to transact.
source_note: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: In Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project (2015), the U.S. Supreme Court confirmed that Fair Housing Act liability can be based on which legal theory, in addition to intentional discrimination?
choice_a: Disparate impact - facially neutral policies or practices that have an unjustified discriminatory effect on a protected class
choice_b: Strict liability for any housing denial
choice_c: Only criminal liability, never civil liability
choice_d: Vicarious liability of tenants for landlord conduct
explanation: The Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act: a facially neutral policy or practice can still violate the Act if it has an unjustified discriminatory effect on a protected class, even without proof of discriminatory intent.
source_note: Texas Dep't of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was enacted in which year, and Title III of the Act primarily governs which type of entity?
choice_a: 1968; private residential dwellings
choice_b: 1990; places of public accommodation and commercial facilities
choice_c: 1988; federally-assisted housing only
choice_d: 2010; employment discrimination only
explanation: The ADA was enacted in 1990. Title III prohibits disability discrimination in places of public accommodation (e.g., retail stores, hotels, restaurants) and requires accessibility in commercial facilities; Title I covers employment and Title II covers state/local government services.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq. (ADA Title III).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: In the real estate context, which of the following areas of an apartment complex is most likely to be subject to the ADA's Title III public accommodation requirements, as distinct from the Fair Housing Act, which primarily governs the dwelling units themselves?
choice_a: A tenant's private bedroom
choice_b: A tenant's private balcony
choice_c: The leasing/rental office and any clubhouse or amenity areas open to the general public
choice_d: The interior of an individually leased unit's kitchen
explanation: The ADA's Title III generally does not reach purely private residential dwelling units (those fall under the Fair Housing Act and, for federally-assisted housing, Section 504), but it does apply to leasing/sales offices, model units used as sales offices, and amenity or common areas that function as places of public accommodation.
source_note: ADA.gov, Title III Regulations; DOJ ADA guidance on rental offices as public accommodations.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under Title III of the ADA, what does 'readily achievable' mean in the context of barrier removal in existing places of public accommodation?
choice_a: Removal that must be completed regardless of cost
choice_b: Removal that is voluntary and can be indefinitely postponed
choice_c: Removal that applies only to newly constructed buildings
choice_d: Removal that is easily accomplishable and able to be carried out without much difficulty or expense
explanation: Under the ADA, existing places of public accommodation must remove architectural barriers when doing so is 'readily achievable' - that is, easily accomplishable and able to be carried out without much difficulty or expense, considering factors like cost and the entity's resources.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 12181(9); ADA Title III regulations, 28 C.F.R. § 36.304.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under Title III of the ADA, which animals must a place of public accommodation, such as a leasing office, generally permit to accompany an individual with a disability?
choice_a: Dogs (and, in some cases, miniature horses) that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the individual
choice_b: Any animal the individual claims provides emotional comfort
choice_c: Only animals that have completed a state-certified training and registration program
choice_d: No animals under any circumstances
explanation: Under ADA Title III, a 'service animal' is defined narrowly as a dog (with a separate provision allowing miniature horses in some circumstances) individually trained to perform tasks for a person with a disability. Staff may ask only two limited questions and cannot require documentation, certification, or registration.
source_note: 28 C.F.R. § 36.104 (ADA service animal definition, effective March 15, 2011).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: How does the ADA's definition of a covered 'service animal' differ from the Fair Housing Act's treatment of 'assistance animals' in housing?
choice_a: They are identical in every respect
choice_b: The ADA's service animal definition is limited essentially to trained dogs (and miniature horses in some cases) performing specific tasks, while the Fair Housing Act's broader 'assistance animal' concept can include other species and animals that provide therapeutic emotional support, not just task-trained work
choice_c: The Fair Housing Act only recognizes cats as assistance animals
choice_d: The ADA covers housing units directly, making the Fair Housing Act's assistance animal provisions redundant
explanation: The ADA's public-accommodation 'service animal' definition is narrower (essentially dogs trained to perform tasks). The Fair Housing Act's 'assistance animal' concept used for reasonable accommodation requests is broader and can include emotional support animals and species beyond dogs, evaluated case-by-case.
source_note: 28 C.F.R. § 36.104; HUD Notice FHEO-2020-01.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, as applied to real estate brokerage, most directly prohibits which of the following?
choice_a: A single brokerage independently setting its own commission rates
choice_b: A broker advertising a listing using the Equal Housing Opportunity logo
choice_c: Agreements between competing brokers or brokerages that unreasonably restrain trade, such as price fixing, market allocation, and group boycotts
choice_d: A broker requiring earnest money on a purchase contract
explanation: The Sherman Antitrust Act (15 U.S.C. §§ 1-2) prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that unreasonably restrain trade, including agreements between competing brokerages to fix prices, allocate markets, or boycott competitors. A single firm independently setting its own rates is not, by itself, a Sherman Act violation.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §§ 1-2 (Sherman Antitrust Act).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Two competing brokerages in the same market secretly agree that neither firm will charge a listing commission below 6%. This is an example of which antitrust violation, and how is it typically treated?
choice_a: Market allocation; legal if disclosed to clients
choice_b: Tie-in arrangement; legal under RESPA
choice_c: Group boycott; legal if approved by the local MLS board
choice_d: Price fixing; treated as a per se illegal violation of the Sherman Act regardless of whether the agreed rate seems reasonable
explanation: An agreement between competing brokerages to set or standardize commission rates is price fixing, which is treated as a per se illegal restraint of trade under the Sherman Act - it is illegal regardless of whether the fixed rate is 'reasonable.' Commission rates must always be independently and unilaterally set by each brokerage and remain negotiable.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; United States v. Socony-Vacuum Oil Co. (per se price-fixing standard).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Several established brokerages in a city agree among themselves to refuse to show properties listed by, or cooperate with, a new discount brokerage entering the market. This conduct is best described as which antitrust violation?
choice_a: Group boycott
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: Blockbusting
explanation: A group boycott occurs when two or more competitors agree to refuse to deal with, or withhold their patronage from, another business (such as a discount brokerage) to reduce or eliminate competition. This is a Sherman Act violation, distinct from the fair-housing concepts of redlining, steering, or blockbusting.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; FTC/DOJ Antitrust Guidelines for real estate professionals.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Two competing real estate brokerages agree that Brokerage A will only list and sell properties on the north side of town while Brokerage B will only operate on the south side, so that neither firm competes for the other's business. This is an example of:
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Market allocation
choice_c: Reasonable accommodation
choice_d: Blockbusting
explanation: Market allocation is an antitrust violation in which competitors agree to divide a market - by geographic territory, customer type, or price range - and refrain from competing in each other's assigned area. It is illegal under the Sherman Act regardless of whether it harms consumers directly, and should not be confused with redlining (a fair-housing lending violation).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A brokerage tells buyers that, in order to have their offer accepted, they must also use the brokerage's affiliated mortgage and title companies. Without addressing any other regulatory scheme, this kind of forced bundling of services is generally analyzed under antitrust law as a potential:
choice_a: Blockbusting scheme
choice_b: Reasonable modification
choice_c: Tie-in (tying) arrangement
choice_d: Exclusive-right-to-sell listing
explanation: A tie-in (or tying) arrangement conditions the sale or availability of one product or service on the buyer's purchase of a separate, distinct product or service. When a brokerage conditions a favorable outcome on using its affiliated settlement service providers, it raises both antitrust tying concerns and, separately, RESPA issues.
source_note: Antitrust tying doctrine under the Sherman Act; general real estate practice guidance on affiliated business arrangements.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What is a key potential consequence for individuals and firms found to have violated the Sherman Antitrust Act through conduct such as price fixing or bid rigging?
choice_a: Only a formal warning letter from the FTC
choice_b: Automatic loss of real estate license with no other penalty
choice_c: No penalty, since antitrust law does not apply to services
choice_d: Criminal penalties, including substantial fines and imprisonment, in addition to civil liability such as treble (triple) damages in private lawsuits
explanation: Sherman Act violations can be prosecuted criminally, exposing individuals to imprisonment and corporations and individuals to substantial fines, and can also give rise to civil antitrust suits in which successful private plaintiffs may recover treble (triple) damages.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §§ 1-2, 15 (criminal penalties and treble damages provisions).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A brokerage's own internal management sets a firm-wide policy that all of its agents will charge a 6% commission on listings. Is this, by itself, a Sherman Antitrust Act violation?
choice_a: No, a single firm's unilateral, independent decision about its own pricing is not a horizontal agreement between competitors and is not, by itself, illegal price fixing
choice_b: Yes, any fixed commission rate is automatically illegal
choice_c: Yes, because commissions must always be exactly the same across all agents in a market
choice_d: No, because antitrust law never applies to real estate
explanation: Antitrust price-fixing violations require an agreement between competitors (a horizontal agreement). A single brokerage's unilateral internal pricing policy for its own agents is not, by itself, an illegal antitrust conspiracy - the illegality arises when competing, independent brokerages agree with one another on pricing.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1 (requires concerted action, not unilateral conduct); FTC guidance on real estate commissions.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under Section 3604(c) advertising rules, an advertisement that states a property is available only to a 'Christian family' or 'no children' would most likely be considered:
choice_a: Legal, as long as the seller personally holds that preference
choice_b: A prohibited discriminatory statement indicating a preference or limitation based on religion and familial status
choice_c: Legal if published only in a niche religious newspaper
choice_d: Legal because advertising is not covered by the Fair Housing Act
explanation: Section 3604(c) prohibits any advertisement indicating a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class, including religion and familial status. Phrases such as 'Christian family' or 'no children' are treated as classic examples of prohibited discriminatory advertising language regardless of the underlying intent or publication venue.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 C.F.R. Part 109.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: HUD's fair housing advertising guidance recommends that real estate advertisers do which of the following to demonstrate a nondiscriminatory advertising policy?
choice_a: Avoid using the Equal Housing Opportunity logo or slogan, since it might draw complaints
choice_b: Only use images of one demographic group to keep advertising simple
choice_c: Include the Equal Housing Opportunity logo, statement, or slogan and avoid human models or visual cues that suggest an exclusive preference for one group
choice_d: Restrict advertising to publications aimed at a single protected class
explanation: HUD encourages the use of the Equal Housing Opportunity logo, statement, or slogan in advertising, and its guidelines caution against using human models or other visual and verbal cues in a manner that suggests a preference for or exclusion of any protected class.
source_note: 24 C.F.R. Part 109, HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A brokerage places its rental listings exclusively in publications and social media channels targeted at one specific ethnic community, and never advertises those same units anywhere else, in order to limit the pool of applicants to that group. This advertising practice is best understood as a form of:
choice_a: Legitimate market segmentation with no fair housing implications
choice_b: A required practice under HUD guidelines
choice_c: A private-club exemption
choice_d: Discriminatory advertisement placement, which can constitute unlawful steering or a Section 3604(c) violation
explanation: HUD's advertising guidance covers not just the words used in an ad, but also discriminatorily selective use of advertising media or content to reach - or avoid reaching - particular groups. Deliberately limiting exposure of listings to one group's media channels can itself constitute unlawful steering or a 3604(c) violation.
source_note: 24 C.F.R. § 109.25 (selective use of advertising media/content).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under Section 3604(c), does the format or medium of an advertisement (print, MLS remarks field, website listing, or social media post) affect whether fair housing advertising rules apply?
choice_a: No; the same discriminatory-language prohibitions apply across all advertising media, including MLS remarks, websites, and social media, and agents remain responsible for compliance regardless of the channel used
choice_b: Fair housing advertising rules apply only to printed newspaper classified ads
choice_c: Digital and social media advertising is entirely unregulated
choice_d: Only advertisements placed directly by the seller (not the agent) are covered
explanation: Section 3604(c)'s prohibition on discriminatory advertising applies across all media and formats - print, digital listings, MLS remarks fields, and social media alike - and agents/brokers are responsible for ensuring compliance regardless of the specific channel or whether a violation was intentional.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD guidance extending advertising rules to digital and social media platforms.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: As a matter of general real estate advertising practice (beyond fair housing law specifically), a licensee who advertises a property for sale should generally:
choice_a: Never disclose that they are a licensed agent, so the ad appears to come from a private seller
choice_b: Ensure the advertisement is truthful, not misleading, and does not obscure the fact that it is placed by a real estate licensee acting in that capacity
choice_c: Use only the seller's personal contact information with no reference to the brokerage
choice_d: Guarantee a specific future resale value in the ad copy
explanation: General real estate advertising practice (reflected in industry ethics standards) requires that advertising be truthful and not misleading, and that licensees clearly present themselves as agents rather than disguising 'blind ads' as private-party listings, which misleads consumers about who they are dealing with.
source_note: General real estate practice principle reflected in NAR Code of Ethics, Article 12 (truthful advertising and disclosure of licensee status).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Fair housing obligations under the Fair Housing Act apply to:
choice_a: Only the sale of homes, not the rental or management of rental housing
choice_b: Only transactions involving a licensed real estate broker
choice_c: Both sales transactions and rental/property management activities, including tenant selection, terms, and services
choice_d: Only single-family homes, not apartment complexes
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's prohibitions apply broadly to both the sale and the rental of dwellings, meaning property managers and rental owners are equally bound by its nondiscrimination requirements in tenant selection, lease terms, and services, not just brokers handling sales.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604 (applies to both 'sale or rental').

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: To reduce fair housing liability, a property management company should apply its tenant screening criteria (credit score, income, rental history, criminal background, etc.) in which manner?
choice_a: Selectively, adjusting the criteria for each applicant based on personal impressions
choice_b: Only to applicants the manager is unsure about
choice_c: Differently depending on the neighborhood where the applicant currently lives
choice_d: Uniformly and consistently to all applicants, regardless of protected class, and documented in writing
explanation: A key fair housing best practice for property managers is to establish written screening criteria and apply them uniformly to every applicant. Inconsistent or selective application of criteria - even if the criteria themselves are neutral - creates strong evidence of disparate treatment based on a protected class.
source_note: HUD guidance on tenant screening practices and disparate treatment.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property manager wants to adopt an occupancy policy limiting the number of people who may live in a unit. Under HUD's longstanding guidance (the 'Keating Memo'), an occupancy standard of two persons per bedroom is generally considered:
choice_a: A reasonable general standard, though it is not an absolute safe harbor and must still be evaluated against factors like unit size and local codes, and cannot be used as a pretext to exclude families with children
choice_b: Automatically illegal because any occupancy limit violates familial status protections
choice_c: Required by federal law in every jurisdiction
choice_d: Irrelevant, since occupancy standards are never subject to fair housing review
explanation: HUD's 1998 'Keating Memorandum' recognized two persons per bedroom as a generally reasonable starting point for occupancy standards, but cautioned that reasonableness depends on factors such as unit and bedroom size, and that occupancy policies cannot be used as a pretext to discriminate against families with children under the familial status provisions.
source_note: HUD General Counsel memorandum on occupancy standards ('Keating Memo,' 1998).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property management company collects security deposits and rent payments on behalf of the owners it represents. As a matter of general trust fund handling practice, the property manager should:
choice_a: Deposit client funds into the company's general operating account to simplify bookkeeping
choice_b: Keep client trust funds (such as security deposits and collected rents) separate from the company's own operating funds and avoid commingling
choice_c: Use client trust funds to cover short-term operating expenses as long as they are repaid eventually
choice_d: Hold all client funds in cash on-site
explanation: A fundamental property management and brokerage trust-account practice is to keep client/trust funds - such as security deposits and collected rents belonging to owners or tenants - segregated from the firm's own operating funds, and never commingled with company or personal funds.
source_note: General real estate brokerage trust account practice, reflected across state real estate license law and standard property management practice.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property manager operating a small owner-occupied duplex hires a licensed leasing agent to handle all showings and lease signings for the vacant unit. Does the 'Mrs. Murphy' owner-occupant exemption from the Fair Housing Act still apply to this rental?
choice_a: Yes, because the building has fewer than four units
choice_b: Yes, as long as the agent is a family member
choice_c: No, because the exemption requires that no real estate broker, agent, or salesperson be used in the transaction, and using a licensed leasing agent removes the exemption
choice_d: No, because duplexes are never eligible for any Fair Housing Act exemption
explanation: The Mrs. Murphy exemption under Section 3603(b)(2) is unavailable once the owner uses the services of a real estate broker, agent, salesperson, or any person in the business of selling or renting dwellings, or uses discriminatory advertising. Hiring a licensed leasing agent to handle the transaction eliminates the exemption.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b); 42 U.S.C. § 3603(c) (exemption unavailable when a broker/agent is used).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A landlord's rental application asks every applicant to state their national origin and religion 'for statistical purposes only,' though the landlord claims this information does not affect the leasing decision. Under the Fair Housing Act, is this practice generally permissible?
choice_a: Yes, because the landlord claims the information will not be used to discriminate
choice_b: Yes, as long as the form is reviewed only by an attorney
choice_c: No, but only if the applicant is later denied housing
choice_d: Generally no; routinely collecting protected-class information not relevant to a legitimate business need creates strong evidence of discriminatory intent and exposes the landlord to liability, even absent proof the data was actually used to deny housing
explanation: Courts and HUD guidance treat the routine collection of protected-class information unrelated to a legitimate, nondiscriminatory business purpose as evidence supporting a discrimination claim, since it creates the opportunity and appearance of discriminatory screening, regardless of the landlord's stated intent.
source_note: HUD guidance on rental applications and protected-class inquiries; general fair housing compliance practice.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which federal civil rights statute, separate from and older than the Fair Housing Act, guarantees all citizens the same right to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real and personal property, and contains no exemptions for race discrimination?
choice_a: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. § 1982)
choice_b: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)
choice_c: The Truth in Lending Act (TILA)
choice_d: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)
explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1866, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 1982, guarantees all citizens the same property rights as white citizens and, as interpreted in Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., contains no exemptions - meaning racial discrimination in real property transactions is illegal under this older statute even in situations exempt from the Fair Housing Act itself.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 1982; Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968).
